text: A finished ETL script doesn't run itself. Something still has to actually kick it off — on a schedule, without you sitting there. On Linux and macOS that's cron; on Windows it's Task Scheduler. This lesson is about getting that wired up correctly.

crontab -e opens your schedule file. Zero 6 star star star means minute 0, hour 6, every day, every month, every weekday — 6 a.m. daily. And that trailing redirect, appending both output and errors to a log file, matters a lot, because cron runs with no terminal attached. Skip that redirect and any output is just gone.

Five fields, always in the same order: minute, hour, day of month, month, and weekday. A star means that field isn't restricted — it matches anything. Something like 1 dash 5 in the weekday field means Monday through Friday. Once you can read these five fields cold, cron stops feeling mysterious.

Windows doesn't have cron, but Task Scheduler does the same job — a Daily trigger, an action that points at python.exe with your script's path as the argument, and critically, 'run whether user is logged on or not,' so it still fires even if nobody's signed in. And yes, it's scriptable from PowerShell too, with New-ScheduledTaskAction and Register-ScheduledTask.

Here's the classic automation trap. A relative path like 'orders.csv' works every time you run the script by hand from its own folder — but a scheduler doesn't start there. It might start in your home directory, or System32. The fix is to always build an absolute path off the script's own location, with os.path.dirname of os.path.abspath of double-underscore file.

Two different logs tell you two different things. The pipeline's own log file — the one from Lesson 39 — tells you whether the script itself succeeded. Grepping cron's syslog, or checking Get-ScheduledTaskInfo on Windows, tells you whether the job was even launched in the first place. A script that never ran leaves an empty pipeline log, not an error in it — so you need both.

Next: keeping secrets out of the script entirely. You've got a scheduled pipeline connecting to a real database now — next lesson covers environment variables and python-dotenv, so a password never has to sit in your code.
